pr_title: Add function to clean up column names with special characters
pr_body:
Changed the backtick quoting functions so that you can also use backtick quoting to use invalid Python identifiers like ones that start with a digit, start with a number, or are separated by operators instead of spaces. 

- [x] closes #27017
- [x] tests added / passed
- [x] passes `black pandas`
- [x] passes `git diff upstream/master -u -- "*.py" | flake8 --diff`
- [x] whatsnew entry

As this builds upon #24955 I think @jreback would be again the right person for the code review.

@jreback 

This PR does not only add the functionality of using special characters in backtick quoted identifiers. It improves on a wide range of issues with my latest PR (#24955). 

To summarize, this PR consists of the following improvements:

* Raise an error when it is not possible to convert a backtick quoted string to a valid Python identifier. (These cases are rare, but it is good to still raise an understandable error.) (`_create_valid_python_identifier`)
* Raise an error when the conversion of the column resolvers to valid Python identifiers creates an ambiguity. This has to do with how Python parses spaces. This issue was already in there with the previous PR, but wasn't handled. Although I doubt someone in the world would ever differentiate its column names based on a difference in whitespace, it is still good to have such an error raised, as it would otherwise pass silently. (`_get_space_character_free_column_resolvers`)
* Moved all code from common.py to expr.py. (I think it is better to have that at one place, I realized.)
* The actual improvement of using special characters in the backtick quoted strings. (`_remove_spaces_column_name` -> `_create_valid_python_identifier`)
* Tests to cover the above.
* The backtick quoted string as well as the column name will undergo the same process (tokenizing and cleaning) so that special cases where tokenizing removes too much whitespace, still get resolved in the end. (see for example #28893)
* Improved documentation that also covers the edge cases.

I think the PR improves on a lot of things, and not only adding more coverage for different cases for the backtick quoted strings. 

Also, keep in mind that we are not expanding the DSL for the .query function. We are only adding more coverage for different cases in naming, i.e. special characters, next to spaces.

Yet another improvement. I was able to fix the problem with the multiple spaces. I just made use of the indices of the token_generator to extract the exact indices of the backtick quoted string. So, you completely circumvent any undesired manipulation done to the tokens. 

This will simplify the PR also because it removes documenting that edge case and catching an error when that occurs (that was a significant portion of code.).

Sorry if this is a silly question @hwalinga, I understand the goal of this is to be able to run something like:
```python
import pandas
df = pandas.DataFrame({'$ amount': [10, 200, 20]})
df.query('`$ amount` < 50')
```
And what you're doing is converting `$ amount < 50` to `_DOLLARSIGN__amount > 50` before the `eval` is executed.

Why don't we execute the `eval` as `locals()['$ amount'] < 50` instead?

@datapythonista 

An interesting observation; I never thought about that. However, upon trying it, I got the an error saying that the function `locals` is not supported by the `query` function. 

I don't know the exact workings of the downstream code, but I think such a solution in which we try to support locals for downstream code might become too complex, also because there are different engines by which the query can be executed. There is python and numexpr, and I don't know what will happen in the future. If more engines will be added we need to support locals for that as well, while this solution will work regardless. 

Therefor, in my view, albeit the current solution is a bit hacky, it does provide a simpler query string for any downstream code working with it.

> @datapythonista
> 
> An interesting observation; I never thought about that. However, upon trying it, I got the an error saying that the function `locals` is not supported by the `query` function.
> 
> I don't know the exact workings of the downstream code, but I think such a solution in which we try to support locals for downstream code might become too complex, also because there are different engines by which the query can be executed. There is python and numexpr, and I don't know what will happen in the future. If more engines will be added we need to support locals for that as well, while this solution will work regardless.
> 
> Therefor, in my view, albeit the current solution is a bit hacky, it does provide a simpler query string for any downstream code working with it.

@hwalinga so the point is this. we *don't* need to actually use numexpr here for non-trivial usages. we can simply execute it directly (this in fact is what ``engine='python'``. I am all for reorganizing the code, but I agree it would be nice to actually simplify this.

So, the proposal is to move the name resolving to the ast tree instead (the parsing used by engine='python'). The ast parser is a very complicated piece of code and there is already a lot of custom stuff in there. The tokenization is much easier and there is not so much custom stuff in that. I think it is not a good idea to move some of the functionality to the ast parser, and here I summed up why:

 * I don't think it is a good idea to bring more customization to the already complex tree parser.

 * I think it is better to keep the code regarding backtick quoting clustered and not to scatter it around with some in the token parsing and some in the tree parsing. I like that is now all in one place in the `parsing.py` file.

 * Backtick quoting is more related to the token parsing. The code now just simplifies the query before it got send to the engine. (It resolves the backtick quoting, and updates the name resolvers.)

 * I think pandas should simplify the query the most as possible before it sends it to the engine, because the engine could be a third party engine. (Like the 'numexpr'.) This will probably also help in the future whenever there is the possibility to add more engines. You want to keep the amount of features of the query that they are processing to a minimum, so that those engines can focus primarily on the processing than on the parsing. So, they only deal with a mostly simple query in addition to the name resolvers, not too much other stuff.

 * Numexpr does not support locals()[]. We can use such a thing only for our own custom parser and that will make this feature only available for engine='python'. This might be not a very big of a deal (most people probably just use the python engine and don't bother with installing numexpr), and I agree we don't have to write overly complicated code to support both. However, we already support both with the current implementation and since 'numexpr' is the default engine it also would not really make sense to not support that one. (It however autofallbacks to python, which I also don't think is a very good idea, but I elaborated on that already in #30005)

 * This would also mean a regression, as 25.3 already supports backtick quoting for both numexpr and python already.

With all this in mind, I think we should just proceed with the current implementation we have now.

> the possibility to add more engines

Is this something we actually anticipate happening?

@jbrockmendel 

I think we don't expect new engines to be added, but with this statement in the readme `Additionally, it has the broader goal of becoming the most powerful and flexible open source data analysis / manipulation tool available in any language.`, I thought query might play a role in that. So, that is just one of the reasons I wanted to keep the query that is send to the engine as simple as possible.

@hwalinga I second that. One more use case besides `this.kind.of.name` is also when a column name starts with a digit (which is not a valid Python variable name), like `60d` or `30d`.

Currently (as of 0.25.1) even using backticks doesn't work with columns starting with a digit.

```python
df.eval("`column 60d` + `column 30d`") # works
df.eval("`60d` + `30d`") # fails
```

It seems that under the hood, Pandas replaces spaces by underscores and removes the backticks like this:

```
`hello there` + `foo bar`
# becomes
hello_there_BACKTICK_QUOTED_STRING + foo_bar_BACKTICK_QUOTED_STRING
# which is a valid Python expression

and

`30d` + `60d`
# becomes
30d_BACKTICK_QUOTED_STRING + 60d_BACKTICK_QUOTED_STRING
# which is NOT a valid Python expression
```

As a solution, one might suggest always prepending a `_` in front of a backticked-column (instead of only appending `_BACKTICK_QUOTED_STRING` like now), like the following:

```
`30d` + `60d`
# would become
_30d_BACKTICK_QUOTED_STRING + _60d_BACKTICK_QUOTED_STRING
# which is a valid Python expression
```

@jreback 

> changing to non python semantics is cause for confusion

I don't think this is right. Datasets' column names (and the people who come up with them) couldn't care less about Python semantics, and it seems reasonable enough to think that Pandas users would expect `eval` and `query` to work out-of-the-box with any kind of dataset column names.

Another way to put it is that the analytics tool (here, Pandas) has to adapt to real-life datasets, instead of the other way around. The "other way around" will simply never happen, and if it doesn't happen either on Pandas' side, then it's up to the Pandas analyst to deal with the nitty-gritty hoops and bumps of dealing with exotic column names. Which is far from ideal.

Thanks for the feedback. 

I can understand jreback's perspective. Allowing all these kind of edge cases brings in quite some **ugly** code to the codebase. Unless you have your own language parser build-in. You aren't really solving it very elegantly. 

Even if we allow for these kind of edge cases to be valid with the aforementioned hacks, there will all kinds of ways to break it. 

Some different approach that has also been discussed was to use uuid instead. That would probably be most elegant, but would make exceptions harder to read. 

Since there are now multiple people having trouble (or expecting too much) from the backticks, maybe the backtick approach is something worth reimplementing, even though the exceptions become harder to read?
